claims.text: TiVNbTa is a refractory high-entropy alloy with superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility.
Trace interstitial oxygen in TiVNbTa promotes phase segregation during thermal aging.
A 1–2 wt% aluminum addition should be introduced during TiVNbTa synthesis.
Aluminum will act as an oxygen scavenger during processing of TiVNbTa.
The aluminum addition will form aluminum-oxygen compounds such as Al2O3.
Aluminum-oxygen compounds will sequester oxygen away from the TiVNbTa metal matrix.
Sequestering oxygen will prevent depletion of oxygen-induced solid-solution strengthening.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen initially contribute to solid-solution strengthening in TiVNbTa.
Thermal-aging-induced phase segregation depletes strengthening interstitials from the TiVNbTa matrix and causes progressive softening.
Aluminum scavenging of residual oxygen will reduce oxygen-driven phase segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Aging TiVNbTa at 700°C causes microstructural evolution and mechanical softening.
Aging at 700°C is representative of jet-turbine service conditions.
After aging at 700°C for 100 hours, aluminum-doped TiVNbTa will have at least 10% higher yield strength than undoped TiVNbTa.
Adding 1–2 wt% aluminum will not significantly degrade room-temperature ductility.
Adding 1–2 wt% aluminum will not significantly increase alloy density.
Excessive aluminum or atypically high oxygen may produce undesirable intermetallic phases or oxides.
Matched aluminum-doped and undoped TiVNbTa samples aged at 700°C for 100 hours provide a controlled test of the hypothesis.
Failure to achieve a 10% yield-strength improvement over the undoped baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says aluminum removes oxygen from the metal matrix while also preventing depletion of oxygen-induced solid-solution strengthening. Removing oxygen into oxides is itself a depletion of matrix oxygen, and the cited evidence identifies such interstitial depletion as the cause of softening.
